abstract.p: Neurodegenerative diseases typically emerge after an extended prodromal period, underscoring the critical importance of initiating interventions during the early stages of brain aging to enhance later resilience. Changes in presynaptic active zone proteins ("PreScale") are considered a dynamic, resilience-enhancing form of plasticity in the process of early, still reversible aging of the Drosophila brain. Aging, however, triggers significant changes not only of synapses but also mitochondria. While the two organelles are spaced in close proximity, likely reflecting a direct functional coupling in regard to ATP and Ca2+ homeostasis, the exact modes of coupling in the aging process remain to understood.

We here show that genetic manipulations of mitochondrial functional status, which alters brain oxidative phosphorylation, ATP levels, or the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), can bidirectionally regulate PreScale during early Drosophila brain aging. Conversely, genetic mimicry of PreScale resulted in decreased oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production, potentially due to reduced mitochondrial calcium (Ca2+) import.

Our findings indicate the existence of a positive feedback loop where mitochondrial functional state and PreScale are reciprocally coupled to optimize protection during the early stages of brain aging.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Global aging leads to a significant increase in the older population, with projections indicating that the number of individuals aged over 65 will exceed 1.6 billion within the next three decades [1]. This demographic shift brings challenges due to age-related cognitive and functional decline, impacting individual independence and placing burdens on families and healthcare systems [1,2]. Aging is closely linked to neurodegeneration, with conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases often considered as a continuum of aging [2,3]. Abnormal protein aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, have been found in the brains of aging individuals [4]. Neurodegenerative diseases often manifest after a lengthy prodromal phase spanning decades, highlighting the importance of initiating interventions during “early brain aging” [5]. Thus, deeper insights into the trajectory of brain aging, especially in early stages, is crucial for a rational design of protective strategies.

Synapses serve as fundamental structures for inter-neuronal signaling and activity transfer, with long-term synaptic plasticity being essential for learning and memory [[6], [7], [8]]. Age-related synaptic abnormalities have been widely documented in rodent brain aging studies [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. Regulatory plasticity mechanisms likely continue to operate stabilizing neural function in early aging but eventually fail in late age [[13], [14], [15], [16]]. Crucially, deficits in synaptic homeostasis signal the emergence of pathological aggregates and contribute to memory impairments in Alzheimer's disease progression [[17], [18], [19]].

Roughly 75–80 % of the brain's energy is devoted to neuronal activity, with synapses consuming nearly half of this amount. Processes such as synaptic vesicle filling, recycling, neurotransmitter release, and plasticity mechanisms involving synaptic protein composition remodeling are energetically demanding [20,21]. Moreover, the precise regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ signaling during synaptic transmission heavily depends on ATP-dependent ion pumps [22,23].

Mitochondria, due to their mobility and energy-providing capabilities, are actively recruited to meet these energy demands and buffer Ca2+ at presynaptic sites [24]. It is thus not surprising that aging-associated changes in mitochondrial functionality are considered major contributors to brain aging [25]. ROS, primarily produced by mitochondria, seemingly play a dual, concentration- and context-dependent role in the aging process [26]. While excessive ROS can lead to oxidative damage, moderate amounts of ROS have been suggested to be signaling molecules that promote longevity [27] and induce restorative sleep [28].

Discerning causal factors from epiphenomenal and potentially protective components adds complexity to investigations of synaptic and mitochondrial changes within presynaptic terminals. Consequently, the rules by which these entities are functionally interconnected along the aging trajectory remains largely enigmatic. The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster in this context serves as a valuable model for aging research, offering a relatively short brain aging process of just a few weeks, integrated with efficient genetic and behavioral analysis tools [29].

Analysis of early Drosophila brain aging has unveiled a brain-wide form of presynaptic plasticity known as "PreScale" [[30], [31], [32]]. PreScale is characterized by an elevation of crucial components of presynaptic active zones that facilitate synaptic vesicle (SV) fusion and transmission. PreScale builds up during early brain aging, to peak at around 50 days of aging, before declining in parallel with the increasing mortality rates in late aging [32]. Genetic interventions targeting PreScale suggest its role in bolstering resilience during early brain aging by coordinating and balancing processes related to sleep, longevity, and memory formation [32].

The findings of this study point towards a direct reciprocal relationship between neuronal mitochondrial function and PreScale-type presynaptic plasticity during early Drosophila brain aging. This interaction appears to be mediated through ROS and Ca2+ signaling, and consequently, allows for a brain state switch that potentially enhances brain resilience against aging. Our findings might instruct the development of protective strategies to optimize early brain aging and mitigate vulnerability to later neurodegeneration.

sec.title: Fly strains and rearing conditions
sec.p: Flies were raised under standard laboratory conditions, with a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, at 65 % humidity, and a temperature of 25 °C. They were fed on a modified Bloomington recipe. For the UAS/Gal4 system, flies were maintained at 29 °C to maximize the effect of the transgenes. All flies used in the experiments were F1 progeny.

w1118 was used as wt (wildtype) control. UAS-dPGC1 was kindly provided by Prof David W Walker (University of California-Los Angeles), UAS-Catalase and UAS-SOD2 were kindly provided by Prof Sean T Sweeney (Department of Biology and Hull York Medical School), UAS-blw RNAi (VDRC #34664, #34663), UAS-IP3R RNAi (BDSC#25937), UAS-RyR RNAi (BDSC#29445), UAS-MCU RNAi (BDSC#42580), UAS-HIF-1α (BDSC#33894) were obtained from the Bloomington Drosophila stock center (BDSC) and Vienna Drosophila Resource Center (VDRC). A brp P [acman] construct [33] was integrated into the 5’ UTR of CG11357 to add more brp gene copy number from wild type (2xBRP) to 4xBRP [32]. Besides, elav-gal4 and tub-gal80ts were the driver lines used in our experiments.

sec.title: Longevity and aging assay
sec.p: Flies were collected on the day of their eclosion. Female and male flies were allowed to mate for 24 h before being separated into individual vials, with 20 flies per vial. Flies were transferred to new vials every other day, including weekends. Each longevity experiment was conducted with at least three biological replicates, with each replicate including 50–70 animals per genotype. In total, approximately 200 flies per genotype per gender were analyzed across the three replicates.

The aging experiment was conducted similarly to the longevity assay. Between 15 and 20 flies were housed in a single vial and transferred to new vials every other day, including weekends, until they reached the anticipated age.

sec.title: Locomotion assay
sec.p: The Negative Gravitaxis Assay [34] measures the locomotor ability of Drosophila based on their natural climbing behavior. In the experiment, 10 test tubes are placed in a concurrent apparatus, and the upper frame is slid to the "testing state," allowing flies to climb from lower to upper tubes. The apparatus is banged five times on a rubber plate to agitate the flies and induce negative gravitaxis. A timer is then started to measure the climbing time. The assay was conducted in complete darkness at 24–25 °C with 40–60 % humidity. Three biological replicates of the locomotion assay were performed, each involving 30–45 flies per genotype for each gender.

sec.title: Paraquat feeding assay and survival curves
sec.p: To expose flies to high oxidative stress, we fed flies with paraquat (Sigma-Aldrich) diluted with 5 % sucrose-ddH2O. Females and males were separated the night before the experiment. 20 flies at specific age were transferred into a small vial with three-layer filter paper soaked with 500 ul 5 % sucrose-5mM paraquat solution, and control flies were kept in the same type of small vials with three-fold filter paper soaked with 500 ul 5 % sucrose solution to avoid thirst and starvation. Flies were transferred to new vials every other day, during which time mortality events were also recorded using the standard form, until all the flies died. Log-rank analysis performed by GraphPad Prism was used to analyze comparison of survival rate.

sec.title: Mitoquinone (mitoQ) supplementation
sec.p: For acute mitoQ (Mitoquinone mesylate, MedChemExpress) administration, 1 mM mitoQ was added to a 5 % sucrose-2% agar medium. When flies reached a desired age, they were transferred from normal food to the 5 % sucrose-2% agar medium with or without mitoQ for a designated time period.

sec.title: H2O2 treatment and western blotting (WB)
sec.p: Prior to the western blot experiment, we exposed flies to concentration gradients of H2O2 (Roth, GmbH, 30 % hydrogen peroxide), varying from 2 %, 10 %, to 20 %, across different time intervals—6, 14, 24, and 48 h. As controls, wild-type flies of the same age were fed a 5 % sucrose solution for corresponding time intervals.

The WB experiment was conducted as previously described [35], 6 female fly brains per group were dissected in hemolymph-like saline solution (HL3). The sample volume equal to 1 brain was loaded on purchased gradient gels (4–20 %) used (BioRad #4561096) and immunoblotted, protein transfer was following the standard procedure. Lastly, membrane was incubated with ECL solution (Thermo Scientific #32132) for 10 min and developed in the dark room with Kodak/GE films. The developed films were scanned by an EPSON V330 scanner in 16-bit grayscale tiff format. Tubulin was used as the loading control to normalize protein intensities by ImageJ software. The following primary antibodies were used: Rabbit anti-BRPD2 (1:20,000, generated by Sigrist lab), rabbit anti-Dlg (1:1000, provided by prof Ulrich Thomas), mouse anti-tubulin (1:10,000, Sigma); Secondary antibodies were used: horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated goat anti-rabbit (1:5000, Jackson ImmunoResearch), HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse (1:5000, Jackson ImmunoResearch)

sec.title: Immunostaining and confocal imaging, image quantification
sec.p: Immunostaining was performed as mentioned in previous experiments [32,36]. Female fly brains were dissected in HL3 solutions and kept on ice before fixation. 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) solution was used to fix dissected brains for 40 min at room temperature (RT). After fixation, brains were washed by 0.7 % PBS-T (PBS with 0.7 % Triton X-100) once then blocked in 0.7 % PBST with 10 % normal goat serum (NGS) for at least 2 h at RT. After blocking, brains were incubated in primary antibodies for at least 48 h at 4 °C. Afterward, brain samples were washed by 0.7 % PBST for 5–6 times on a shaker and then incubated in secondary antibodies for 24 h in darkness. Followed by 5–6 times washing again, brains were mounted with Vectashield and stored in darkness at 4 °C overnight. The following primary and secondary antibodies were used: primary antibodies: mouse anti-BRPNC82 (1:50, invitrogen), mouse anti-ATP5A (1:1000, invitrogen), rabbit anti-COXIV (1:500, invitrogen). Secondary antibodies: goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 633 (1:400, invitrogen), goat anti-mouse Alexa 488 (1:400, invitrogen) and goat anti-mouse Cy5 (1:400, invitrogen).

Images were acquired by a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems). 1024 × 1024 images were scanned at 600 Hz using 4x line, acquisition settings to avoid saturation were set constantly for all groups of each immunostaining. ImageJ (Fiji) software was utilized to analyze acquired images. Confocal stacks were merged into a single z-plane by using the average projection function, the region of central brain (region of interest (ROI)) in average projected image for one brain was manually chosen using free-hand function in ImageJ. The fluorescence intensity of ROI was measured and normalized to the area of the central brain in control group.

sec.title: MitoTimer staining assay
sec.p: The fluorescent reporter protein MitoTimer is targeted to the mitochondrial matrix and exhibits color shifts from Green to Red [37].For MitoTimer staining, female fly brains were dissected in HL3 and kept on ice. Following the fixation, the brains were washed three times with PBS, then directly mounted with Vectashield and stored at 4 °C overnight. Images were acquired by a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope. Excited by 488 nm laser, emission captured for the green fluorescence is collected in the 497–531 nm range, while red fluorescence emission is collected in the 583–695 nm range.

sec.title: Measurement of mitochondrial respiration using seahorse XFe96 analyzer
sec.p: After anesthetized on ice, adult fly brains were dissected in assay medium made by supplemented Schneider's medium (ThermoFisher #21720024) containing 1 mM sodium pyruvate to boost mitochondrial oxidative respiration, as depicted previously [35,38]. The hydration of a seahorse XF96 sensor cartridge with 200ul calibrant (Seahorse XF Calibrant Solution 500 mL #100840-000) was performed one day prior to the assay at 25 °C. Followed the protocol of single brain seahorse assay described earlier [39,40]. 20ul assay medium containing single dissected brain was added to an Agilent 96-well cell plate (Agilent, 102416-100), single brain was sunk to the bottom of the well and located in the center of the three raised spheres by a probe. One micro-restrainer with plastic ring side facing towards was pushed to the bottom by a probe to restrict the position of fly brain. The manufacturing process of micro-restrainer was described previously [41]. Extra 160ul assay medium was added to the well. The loading of compounds (Oligomycin: complex V inhibitor; FCCP: proton gradient uncoupler; Antimycin A & Rotenone: complex I, III inhibitor) with modified concentration and calibration of the cartridge sensor were performed on the same day of the assay. Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was measured by the XFe96 analyzer at a suitable temperature for Drosophila. After the assay, the medium was carefully removed, leaving each brain at the bottom of its respective well. The brains were then digested using RIPA lysis buffer (ThermoFisher#89900) for subsequent protein quantification. The OCR was normalized to the protein levels measured by the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit.

sec.title: Mitochondrial DNA measurement
sec.p: As noted earlier [35], the total DNA from 10 adult female brains per genotype were extracted with the NucleoSpin Tissue kit (Macherey-nagel GmbH). MtDNA content was quantified by taking ratio between a mitochondrial-encoded cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI) and nuclear-encoded glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) (mtDNA/nDNA) using quantitative real time PCR. Primer sequences were reported in a previous experiment [42]. Three independent biological replicates were pooled together for data analysis.

sec.title: Measurement of ATP level using luminescent cell Viability assay
sec.p: For each genotype, 15 female fly heads were homogenized in 100 μL of Glo lysis buffer (Promega #E2661) and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen, following protocols established by previous assays [43,44]. Homogenates were diluted 1/20 with the Glo lysis buffer and mixed with the luminescent solution (CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay/Cell TiterGlo 2.0 Assay, Promega). Luminescence intensity was measured with a plate reader (M200 P infinite Pro). The luminescent signal was normalized to protein levels in each well, which were quantified using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Fisher #23227). Data from 2 to 4 independent experiments were pooled together for analysis.

sec.title: Amplex Red hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) assay
sec.p: The Amplex Red Assay [45] was performed to quantify the levels of ROS in Drosophila heads. For every 1 ml of HL3 medium, 5 μl Amplex Red reagent (50uM) (Amplex Red hydrogen Peroxide/Peroxidase Assay kit, Thermo Fisher, #22188) and 10ul HRP (10u/ml) were added. Both female and male fly heads were measured. 5 fly heads were quickly added to 200 μl of the reagent mixture and then pulverized using a homogenizer. After homogenization, the samples were vortexed and swiftly centrifuged, followed by incubation at 25 °C for 90 min in darkness. Afterward, the samples were vortexed again, and 80 μl of the reacted solution was aliquoted into the wells of a 96-well plate. The absorbance was measured using a microplate reader (M200 Pro Infinite), equipped for excitation in the range of 530–560 nm. The absorbance rate was corrected with protein levels, quantified by Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Fisher #23227). The Amplex Red reagent alone was used to subtract background interference, and duplicates from two to three independent biological experiments were pooled together.

sec.title: MitoSOX staining
sec.p: Fly brains were dissected in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and incubated in 20 μM MitoSOX (Invitrogen, M36008) for 10 min, followed by three washes with 1X PBS to remove unbounded dye. Samples were then immediately mounted on glass coverslips with vectashield® antifade mounting medium and imaged using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope, capturing z-stacks across each sample. The total average fluorescence intensity for each brain was quantified using ImageJ.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software. When data conformed to a normal distribution, as verified by the Shapiro–Wilk test, the Student's t-test was used to assess differences between two groups. For multiple comparisons, a one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction was applied. p < 0.05 was considered as significant, and the number of Asterisk was listed to show the strength of significance (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: To test for direct causal relations between neuronal mitochondrial performance and age-associated presynaptic changes (“PreScale”), we first sought to genetically mimic mitochondrial performance changes associated with early aging, and then analyze potential consequences on the synaptic level.

sec.title: Provoking age-typical changes of mitochondrial function triggers premature PreScale
sec.p:
During the period of Drosophila "early brain aging," spanning from eclosion to an age of about 30 days, we confirmed a progressive decline of brain ATP levels in our aging flies via a luminescence assay [43,44] (Fig. 1a), which was accompanied by an increase in hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) levels (Fig. 1b), detected via a modified Amplex Red H2O2 assay [45]. To further validate age-related changes in mitochondrial ROS, we directly quantified mitochondrial ROS levels in the brains of 5-day, 15-day, and 30-day-old flies using mitoSOX Red staining [46,47]. Indeed, we observed an age-dependent increase in mitochondrial ROS levels in fly brains (Fig. 1c). We thus continued by asking whether such functional changes observed in early fly brain aging might be able to tune PreScale in Drosophila brain.Fig. 1

Previous work has shown that a knockdown (KD) of ATP synthase complex subunit α (ATP5A alias Bellwether (blw)) decreases brain ATP levels and induces ROS accumulation in the larval fat body [48,49]. We thus established a pan-neuronal (elav-gal4 driver line) KD of blw via RNA interference (RNAi) in combination with tubulin-gal80ts, restricting the RNAi knockdown to the adult stage (by transferring adult flies from 18 °C to 29 °C post eclosion). ATP5A/Blw KD provoked a significant reduction of Blw protein signal in stainings of 15d-old flies compared to isogenic controls (Fig. S1). Indeed, both mitochondrial basal respiration and ATP levels were markedly reduced in 15d-old fly blw KD animal brains as compared to isogenic controls of the same age (Fig. 1d and e). Additionally, we measured locomotion to assess the physical fitness of the flies. Indeed, neuronal blw knockdown resulted in a marked impairment in locomotion compared to controls (Fig. 1f). Moreover, flies with pan-neuronal blw KD also suffered from a significantly reduced lifespan (Fig. 1g and h). Finally, we analyzed a possible relation to PreScale. Indeed, our pan-neuronal knock-down of blw resulted in the PreScale-typical brain-wide elevation of BRP intensity relative to isogenic controls in 15-day-old fly brain (Fig. 1i).

Hence, an exacerbation of the age-associated mitochondrial changes by a “genetic mimicry” (blw KD) is effective in provoking PreScale to an extent significantly higher than typical for early aging (15 days).

sec.title: Genetic rejuvenation of mitochondria attenuates early aging-associated PreScale
sec.p:
We next sought to in reverse test whether active age-protection of brain mitochondrial function might be able to delay the onset of PreScale. In order to identify a mechanistic avenue to specifically age-protect mitochondria, we also measured the age-related mitochondrial turnover by neuronally expressing the “MitoTimer” construct [37,50]. Measuring the red to green MitoTimer ratio here allows for a quantification of relative changes in mitochondrial turnover [51] (Fig. 2a). Indeed, red to green fluorescence ratios significantly increased in 15d-old fly brains compared to their 5d-old isogenic siblings (Fig. 2b and c), indicative of a decreased mitochondrial turnover in Drosophila brains under early aging brain.Fig. 2

We wondered whether in reverse boosting the biosynthetic supply of mitochondrial proteins might allow to delay their functional decay with age. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma coactivator (PGC1) is thought to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis through the co-activation of nuclear transcription factors and is required for the proper expression of many mitochondrial proteins [52]. To address the consequences of a brain-specific activation of PGC-1, we crossed a UAS-dPGC1 transgene to an elav-gal4 pan-neuronal driver and raised the flies at 29 °C to maximize the expression of PGC-1 [53,54]. To ensure full comparability between genetic groups, we before backcrossed the dPGC1 inducible transgene for six generations into isogenic w1118 control background. MitoTimer fluorescence indicated that neuronal PGC1 overexpression resulted in a “juvenation” of mitochondria during early brain aging (measured at 15d) (Fig. 2d). Moroever, elav/dPGC1 flies (15d-old) displayed significantly elevated level of mitochondrial respiration (Fig. 2e) and higher total brain ATP levels than the controls (Fig. 2f). Finally, we quantified mitochondrial DNA amounts as additional readout of PGC1 effects on fly brains. Mitochondrial DNA/nuclear DNA ratio determined via quantitative real-time PCR [55] revealed distinctly increased amounts of mitochondrial DNA normalized to amounts of nuclear DNA (nDNA) in 10d elav/dPGC1 flies and presented a higher tendency in 15d elav/dPGC1 flies relative to control flies at the same age (Fig. 2g and h). Furthermore, we assessed the locomotor ability of elav/dPGC1 flies. While a slight improvement in climbing was observed in 15d elav/dPGC1 flies (Fig. S3), neuronal PGC1 activation in older flies (30 days) enhanced climbing ability compared to controls (Fig. 2i and j). We then monitored the lifetime of elav/dPGC1 and corresponding controls. Survival curve analysis reported a significantly extended lifespan of elav/dPGC1 male flies (Fig. 2k). Thus, pan-neuronal overexpression of Drosophila PGC1 apparently allows to protect mitochondria from normally occurring decay typical for advancing age [35].

Finally, we performed BRP immunofluorescence staining. Notably, neuronal PGC1 overexpression significantly reduced brain BRP staining intensity in early aging brains compared to isogenic controls (Fig. 2l).

In summary, these findings suggest the existence of a tunable and targetable axis in which mitochondrial function directly modulates BRP levels in adult brains, potentially regulating lifespan and behavioral phenotypes.

sec.title: Exogeneous ROS provokes acute PreScale in Drosophila brain
sec.p: So far, we established evidence that the functional performance of neuronal mitochondria can execute bidirectional control over PreScale in early Drosophila brain aging. We next probed for putative signals conveying information concerning the mitochondrial state to the presynaptic sites.

Administering PQ to Drosophila evaluates the animals' resistance against oxidative stress [56]. Based on the survival curve under PQ feeding, neuronally silencing blw reduced the resilience of flies against oxidative challenges, while pan-neuronal overexpression of dPGC-1 enhanced the ability of flies to tolerate oxidative stress in male flies (Fig. 3e and f).

To explore whether chronically quenching ROS affected PreScale, we employed genetic approaches by pan-neuronally overexpressing (at 29 °C) the “antioxidant enzymes” catalase (Cat) and Superoxide Dismutase2 (SOD2) [57]. Immuno-histological quantification displayed a significant reduction of BRP fluorescence intensity in 15d fly brains of Cat and SOD2 overexpressing animals compared to isogenic wildtype flies of identical age (Fig. 3g). To determine whether pan-neuronal reduction of mitochondrial ROS could reverse the BRP phenotype triggered by neuronal blw KD, we analyzed BRP intensity in pan-neuronal blw KD flies with and without SOD2 overexpression. Remarkably, neuronal SOD2 activation successfully restored BRP intensity in blw KD fly brains to control levels (Fig. 3h). Thus, boosting the neuronal antioxidant capacity seemingly relaxes the necessity for PreScale at the early stages of Drosophila brain aging, and ROS levels might be causally involved in triggering PreScale.

To investigate the coupling of dynamic ROS level changes with PreScale, we fed varying concentration of H2O2 (2 %,10 %,20 %) to young wild-type flies. Using western blots (WB), we monitored PreScale-related changes by tracking the level of pre- and post-synaptic proteins: BRP and Discs large (Dlg), the homolog of the mammalian scaffold protein PSD95 [58,59]. Protein levels were analyzed across multiple time points (6h, 14h, 24h) following H2O2 feeding in 5 % sucrose solution.

In our WB experiments, even the lowest H2O2 concentration (2 %) applied over 6 h triggered BRP upregulation (Fig. 4a). Consequently, we used 2 % H2O2 for all subsequent analyses. We observed that both BRP and Dlg levels began to increase at 6 h, peaked around 12–14 h, and returned to baseline at 24 h (Fig. S5). To confirm this trend, we performed a quantitative WB analysis at continuous time points (6h, 14h, 24h, 48h) using 2 % H2O2. This analysis validated the observed pattern, showing that BRP and Dlg levels continued to decline after 24 h, falling below pre-treatment levels by 48 h (Fig. 4b). Nonlinear fitting via quadratic regression concurrently indicated that BRP and Dlg level peaked at approximately 12h (Fig. 4c). To corroborate these findings, we also performed brain immunostaining using BRPNC82 antibody, which revealed a significant increase in BRP level following 6-h feeding with 2 % H2O2 (Fig. 4d and e).Fig. 4

Finally, we tested whether quenching mitochondrial ROS might be able to reversibly tune PreScale. Thus, we fed flies with mitoquinone (mitoQ), a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant [60]. Indeed, mitoQ supplementation effectively reduced BRP protein levels in both aging flies (30d) as well as 15d neuronal blw KD fly brains relative to controls (Fig. S8).

In summary, acute ROS stress over a few hours is sufficient to trigger PreScale, whereas prolonged ROS exposure eventually leads to a decline in PreScale. Our results suggest that mitochondrial ROS play a significant role in regulating PreScale.

sec.title: Genetically-triggered “PreScale” re-programs brain mitochondria
sec.p: Interaction between mitochondria and presynaptic activity might not be unidirectional, as changes in synaptic activity influence mitochondrial behavior and efficiency [61]. Therefore, we investigated a potential reciprocal relationship between PreScale and mitochondria by adding an extra brp genomic transgene copy, which results in a moderate BRP increase similar to PreScale observed in early brain aging [32]. This allowed us to assess the impact of genetically induced PreScale on mitochondrial function in young animals.

Mitochondrial Complex IV/cytochrome c oxidase IV (COXIV) and Complex V/ATP synthase are two crucial components involved in oxidative respiration and ATP production [62]. To investigate whether the levels of COXIV and ATP5A were altered in the 3xBRP scenario, we performed immunohistochemical analyses targeting COXIV and ATP5A proteins. The analyzed results revealed a discernible reduction in ATP5A intensity, while COXIV level remained unchanged in the brains of 3xBRP flies compared to the isogenic control flies (Fig. 5f-k).

In the 3xBRP fly brain, proton transfer might be interrupted as a consequence of attenuated ATP synthase function, potentially leading to increased ROS production (“reverse electron transport ROS release; [63,64]). Henceforth, we assessed ROS levels and ROS susceptibility in young 3xBRP and wild-type animals. Both, Amplex Red assay and mitoSOX staining revealed a notable increase in mitochondrial ROS level in the heads of 3xBRP flies (Fig. 5l and m). Surprisingly, 3xBRP flies, which exhibited higher ROS levels in their brains, showed increased resilience to oxidative stress compared to their wild-type counterparts, as evidenced by higher survival rates following PQ feeding (Fig. 5n and o). Potentially, the elevated ROS levels observed in the heads of 3xBRP flies might trigger a hormetic response which would facilitate beneficial and adaptive responses against external threats, such as higher oxidative stress [65,66].

sec.title: Mitochondrial Ca2+ influx may mediate PreScale-induced mitochondrial reprogramming
sec.p: The uptake of mitochondrial Ca2+ is meant to be constrained by the concentration of cytosolic Ca2+ [68,69]. Accordingly, at the synaptic terminal, the Ca2+ elevations associated with continued action potential arrival might be linked to mitochondria functionality via presynaptic Ca2+. Moreover, the influx of mitochondrial Ca2+ may trigger the mitochondrial remodeling we observed upon triggering PreScale in Drosophila brain.

Apart from mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is majorly involved in intracellular Ca2+ storage and buffering [70]. The inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (IP3Rs) and Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) represent the distinct types of ER Ca2+ releasing channels. To determine the relevance of different Ca2+ sources to PreScale, we also pan-neuronally knocked down IP3Rs and RyRs (by combining UAS-IP3R RNAi and UAS-RyR RNAi lines with elav-Gal4). Notably, the RNAi lines targeting IP3R, RyR and MCU which we used in our investigations have shown to effectively reduce the corresponding proteins [71,72]. The immunostaining analysis revealed minimal changes in BRP levels when inhibiting either IP3Rs or RyRs pan-neuronally, compared to appropriate controls (Fig. 6f and g). Thus, an impairment of mitochondrial Ca2+ influx, rather than changes of ER Ca2+ release, seems to be causally coupled with the advent of PreScale.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Establishing mechanistic connections between neuronal subcellular regulations across the aging trajectory is crucial, with mitochondria and synapses being particularly relevant entities. During “early” still reversible phases of aging, brains likely undergo protective regulations before ultimately transiting into irreversible aging after passing critical restriction and transition points. Identifying and characterizing the interplay of relevant signals, which are often interpreted in a concentration- and aging context-dependent fashion, is imperative in this regard.

Our previous studies highlighted brain-wide increases in presynaptic active zone proteins (here referred to as "PreScale") (Gupta V.K., 2016; [32]) and a significant decrease in mitochondrial respiration [35] in the first 30 days of Drosophila brain aging (“early aging”). As mentioned above already, genetic interventions targeting PreScale point towards its involvement in promoting resilience during early brain aging by coordinating and balancing sleep, longevity, and memory formation processes [32]. However, after passing a critical point around 50 days of age, PreScale declines, coinciding with rising mortality rate in late aging.

Changes in mitochondrial functionality are believed to be crucially involved in the pace of the aging process itself and of aging-associated disorders [73]. In this study, we revealed a direct coupling between mitochondrial functional status and presynaptic “PreScale” plasticity during the early stage of Drosophila brain aging, suggesting a bidirectional relationship of both entities (model Fig. 7a). We genetically manipulated the transcription coactivator PGC1 which promotes mitochondrial biogenesis [74]. Pan-neuronal stimulation of the PGC1 rejuvenated brain mitochondria and simultaneously delayed the onset of aging-associated PreScale (Fig. 2 and model Fig. 7b). Notable in this regard, age-delaying effects of PGC-1 have been illustrated in both Drosophila and mammalian models. In mouse, activation of PGC1alpha in skeletal muscles protected from sarcopenia in aged male animals [75]. In Drosophila, digestive tract targeted overexpression of PGC1 delays age-related alterations in the intestine and prolongs the organismal lifetime [42]. Similarly, spermidine supplementation, an established “anti-aging paradigm” [76], protects mitochondrial functions from aging [35] and at the same time blocks PreScale during early aging [30,31].Fig. 7
A putative model to elucidate the reciprocal relationship between mitochondrial functionality and “PreScale”
(a). ROS and Ca2+ as crucial signaling entities might establish a positive feedback loop between “PreScale” and mitochondria. “PreScale” modifies neuronal activity from a bursting to a tonic pattern. Consequently, in brains with elevated PreScale, peaks of mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake at presynaptic terminals may be attenuated, leading to reduced metabolic activity and triggering a feedback response
(b). The age-related alterations of mitochondrial state and “PreScale”: Neuronal blw KD exacerbates mitochondrial decay and provokes premature “PreScale”, pushing the early-aging brain toward a later stage. Conversely, pan-neuronal over-expression of PGC1 rejuvenates mitochondrial function and delays the increase of “PreScale”, steering the early-aging brain toward a younger stage.Fig. 7

Our genetic and pharmacological interventions highlighted mitochondrial production of ROS, particularly H2O2, as potential signals for signaling the mitochondrial functional status to the mechanisms controlling presynaptic plasticity (model Fig. 7a). The proposition that ROS, and likely particularly mitochondrial ROS levels, serves as a physiological trigger of PreScale is supported by several findings of this study: i) increased brain mitochondrial ROS levels during early brain aging (Fig. 1c); ii) genetic reduction of ATP synthase subunit 5A led to elevated mitochondrial ROS levels and triggered premature PreScale in young brains (Fig. 3a–b and 1i); iii) feeding moderate concentrations of H2O2 triggered within 6 h prominent PreScale (Fig. 4a); and iv) mitoQ supplementation reversed the increase of PreScale in aging flies and neuronal blw KD fly brains (Fig. S8); v) pan-neuronal overexpression of Catalase and SOD2 reduced the extent of PreScale in early aging (Fig. 3g).

These results raise intriguing questions about the molecular mechanisms underpinning the connection between ROS and PreScale, as well as the physiological significance of this interaction. It is worth noting that sleep deprivation has also been shown to induce changes in BRP levels [58,77,78], which are strikingly similar to those observed in conditions induced by aging or by excessive ROS formation. This observation suggests a significant overlap in the pathways activated under stress conditions such as lack of sleep and those activated during the aging process or in response to oxidative stress, further highlighting the complex interplay between sleep patterns, cellular stress responses, and neuronal plasticity [58,[78], [79], [80]]. Notably, a direct mechanistic connection between sleep loss, ROS accumulation, and compensatory sleep via the potassium channel regulatory subunit Hyperkinetic was demonstrated in sleep-controlling neurons of the Drosophila brain [28]. Besides, PreScale triggers additional sleep and also prolongs the lifetime of Drosophila [77,79], suggesting a ROS-PreScale axis in regulating brain adaptive and protective changes connecting sleep homeostasis and aging.

We would like to emphasize that a brief 6-h exposure to ROS was sufficient to trigger PreScale. However, it is not yet clear whether these effects are directly mediated by ROS acting within the brain. While the precise molecular pathways linking ROS treatment and PreScale activation remain to be determined, this response showing timing dynamics similar to those observed in sleep loss [58]. ROS-induced hormetic responses, wherein low ROS levels trigger adaptive stress response, have been documented to enhance lifespan [81]. In this regard, longevity-promoting effects of mild genetic attenuation of mitochondrial complex I in Drosophila muscle has been found to be mediated by the release of mitochondrial ROS [82]. Moreover, neuronal ROS serve as an obligatory signal for neuronal activity-dependent increases in bouton number and induces overgrowth of larval neuromuscular junctions [83,84]. Interestingly, the ROS-induced JNK-AP-1 pathway is proven to be essential for this pronounced synaptic overgrowth [45,83], and ROS signaling might potentially regulate PreScale by activating transcription factors such as AP-1. Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1 (HIF-1) has been shown to influence synaptic transmission and plasticity in response to oxidative stress [85,86]. To explore whether ROS-mediated HIF-1α regulation might also modulate PreScale, we pan-neuronally silenced HIF-1α in fly brains and performed BRP staining. However, this genetic intervention did not affect BRP protein levels. Furthermore, BRP intensity still increased noticeably following acute H₂O₂ induction in HIF-1α KD animals (Fig. S9). These findings suggest that HIF-1α is not involved in triggering PreScale. Elucidating the interplay among ROS signaling, synaptic plasticity and regulation of survival and sleep behavior will be a crucial avenue towards deciphering the intricate mechanisms underlying (early) brain aging.

Unexpectedly, we found that mimicking PreScale (3xBRP) resulted in increased levels of brain ROS consistent with reduced oxidative phosphorylation rates (Fig. 5). Indeed, increased ROS signaling appears to bi-directionally interact between PreScale and mitochondrial status. Shifting towards slightly increased ROS levels within the early aging process might initiate a brain “state switch” of consolidated PreScale using a positive feedback loop (model Fig. 7a).

Mechanistically, we identified a drop in ATP5A levels in the 3xBRP animals, which might directly contribute to the mitochondrial phenotype characterized by reduced oxidative phosphorylation and lowered ATP levels, as well as increased ROS production, in these brains (Fig. 5). How changes in mitochondrial protein composition in response to the upregulation of presynaptic active zone proteins remains an intriguing question. Interestingly, activating PreScale genetically does not majorly increase single action potential synaptic transmission. Instead, it primarily alters short-term synaptic plasticity as shown by electrophysiological analyses of neuromuscular junctions (see Fig. S4 in Ref. [77]). Additionally, animals with increased brp copy numbers exhibit reduced overall activity levels, indicated by lower calcium-dependent nuclear LexA import (“CaLexA”) in Drosophila neurons. Moreover, in vivo patch clamp recordings of sleep center neurons further revealed that PreScale modifies activity patterns in sleep-regulating neurons, shifting from bursting to tonic firing (Fig. 2 in Ref. [32]). We hypothesize that elevated PreScale attenuates mitochondrial calcium (Ca2+) uptake at presynaptic terminals, reducing metabolic activity and initiating a feedback response (model Fig. 7a). Supporting this, genetic downregulation of MCU robustly induced PreScale, suggesting that PreScale dampens mitochondrial metabolism by limiting Ca2+ influx through the MCU.

In conclusion, PreScale and mitochondrial metabolism appear to interact reciprocally, synchronizing with neuronal activity to balance trade-offs among survival, sleep, and memory formation. ROS and Ca2+ emerge as crucial signaling entities, potentially forming a positive feedback loop between PreScale and mitochondria, thereby enhancing brain resilience during early aging in the Drosophila brain (model Fig. 7a). Exploring this complex interplay underscores the interconnectedness of mitochondrial metabolic status and presynaptic plasticity in the aging brain, offering promising insights into therapeutic avenues for fostering healthy brain aging.
